newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh experts eye potential in Himalayan region.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh experts eye potential in Himalayan region.

text.p: The Asian region bounded by major Himalayan rivers has vast potential for development despite widespread poverty and rampant disasters, Bangladeshi experts said on Wednesday.

"The scope for maximising the use of natural resources are enormous for generation of cheap hydropower, augmentation of the dry season flows of the main river system, navigation, trade and commerce," water expert Amjad Hossain Khan told a seminar.
The seminar focused on the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna (GBM) region, which includes Bangladesh, Bhutan, Nepal and parts of India and China.
"The GBM region has tremendous opportunities for development," said Khan, a member of Bangladesh's national water council headed by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina.
"The region has fertile land, good rainfall and a wide network of rivers for agriculture production," he said.

"It (the region) is beset with poverty and severe environmental degradation but rich in natural resources like water. There is hope for the future development of the region in an integrated manner," Khan said.

Hafiz G.A. Siddiqi, president of the Bangladesh chapter of the Rome-based Society for International Development, said: "This region is prone to natural disasters. It is one of the poorest areas in the world with more than two-thirds of the population living on less than $1 a day.
"But it has vast reserves of natural gas, coal and immense hydropower potentials to make it survive in good health," Siddiqi said.
Qazi Kholiquzzaman Ahmad of Bangladesh Unnayan Parishad (development council) said: "The common resources in the GBM region...can be harnessed through cooperative efforts for common benefits."
The seminar follows criticism by Bangladeshi opposition parties that a 30-year treaty signed with India recently for sharing water of the Ganges river was a "sell out" to Indian interests.

Water resources Minister Abdur Razzak told parliament on Wednesday that not enough water had so far flowed into Bangladesh since the treaty was signed in December 1996, but he predicted conditions would change in the future.

"It is correct that we did not get water as per the treaty. But the reason was a lack of rain in the upstream of the Ganges while the ice on the mountain melted less," he said, replying to comments by an opposition legislator.
"When both conditions will improve, we will have plenty of water."
Razzak said Bangladesh and India would shortly attempt to sign agreements on sharing flows from nearly 150 other rivers.
